fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Body Is the Root, Not the Prison", "body": "Chance Garton opens by reading from Tsarion's book Disciples of the Mysterium, the passage arguing that incorporeal minds do indeed exist within corporeal bodies, and Tsarion contends that severing the two is the first cut made by what Garton calls the priest-archies, the seed of divide and conquer inside a single consciousness. Tsarion argues that many spiritual paths begin as flight from the body, calling the relationship necrophilous, and warns of seekers with their head in the stars who have lost their root. He allows hatha yoga as body centered, and cites Alvin Boyd Kuhn on what Kuhn called the cult of mortification."}, {"title": "The Contrarium and the Rescue of German Idealism", "body": "Tsarion explains the contrarium, his own word for an originary disharmony that he says makes consciousness and life possible, and traces it through Jacob Boehme's dark light and white light, Meister Eckhart, Kant, Fichte and Hegel. He argues Fichte, not Hegel, coined thesis, antithesis and synthesis, and calls Hegel the most misinterpreted philosopher who ever lived, claiming leftist Hegelians dumped his metaphysics and kept a few political scraps. Tsarion says Hegel's real worry was the corrosion of the mitwelt, or society, and that alienation was his most used word. He points to his own books Path of the Fool and Disciples of the Mysterium."}, {"title": "Mysterium: The Ideas We Hold About Ideas", "body": "Tsarion defines mysterium as the false idea generated about reality, which then breeds further ideas about ideas in religion, politics and daily life. His remedy is apophatic method, a continual self-critique he says should be taught to children rather than left to chance, and he insists everything he teaches has been double and triple critiqued. Applied to science, he invokes Thomas Kuhn on paradigms, and names Charles Tart, Iain McGilchrist, Rupert Sheldrake and Michael Cremo as credentialed dissenters. Garton reads Tsarion's line that without a rational vision of ourselves as perfect beings, psychology and psychiatry will ultimately lead us nowhere."}, {"title": "Gnosticism, Hermeticism and the Wealthy Converts", "body": "In the second hour Tsarion separates Gnosticism, which he calls world negating and psychotic at its core, from Hermeticism, which he describes as body centered, earth centered and right brained. He walks through the Nag Hammadi library found in the 1940s, Bishop Irenaeus as the earliest source for the word, and the confusion with the Essenes, Mandeans and Ebionites, criticising GRS Mead, Stephan Hoeller and Manly P Hall for conflating the two traditions. He then claims a wealthy Gnostic set, naming the head of the airline KLM, adopted an aversion therapy strategy: saturate the world with sex, drugs and rock and roll until people recoil from it."}, {"title": "Simulation, Armoring and the Return to Selfhood", "body": "Garton reads an article about Princeton physicist Hong Qin, whose AI algorithm is said to bypass physical law and go straight from data to data, and links simulation theory, the cyberpunk tarot, Elon Musk and Ray Kurzweil to a digital demiurge. Tsarion answers with Wilhelm Reich, describing emotional plague and ocular armoring, and argues the Gnostic is fleeing not the planet but himself. Garton then takes the 1828 Webster's definition of simulation, feigning to be what one is not, calling hypocrisy psychic self-murder. His long solo outro closes with Lao Tzu, the Tao, and the pun that all one and all alone differ by one letter."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: This episode was removed from YouTube a few months ago for no clear reason, so it's time to dust it off and present it in its entirety, with the Plus+ extension free for all.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Legendary lore-master Michael Tsarion joins Innerverse to discuss Disciples of the Mysterium, a book about finding Selfhood in a society lost to collectivist dogma. Michael has been researching and writing on conspiracy topics for over 30 years, and in this episode we sum up his crucial conclusions on psychology, philosophy, and the infectious cult of artificial gnosis.
